topic: Flow on Android: stateIn, lifecycle collection & testing

questions.question: What does `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` do that plain `collectAsState()` doesn't?
options: It stops collecting below STARTED, so a backgrounded app does no work
It converts the flow into a StateFlow shared with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)
It collects the flow on Dispatchers.IO and posts each value back to the main thread
It saves the latest value so that the state is restored after the process is killed
questions.explanation: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` collects only while the lifecycle is at least `minActiveState` (STARTED by default) and restarts when it comes back. `collectAsState` keeps collecting as long as the composable is in the composition, even in the background. It does not change dispatchers, share the flow or persist anything.

questions.question: `lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { render(it) } }` in an Activity's `onCreate` stops collecting when the app goes to the background.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `lifecycleScope` is only cancelled when the lifecycle is DESTROYED, so this keeps collecting (and doing work, maybe even touching views) while the app is in the background. Wrap the collection in `repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED)` to stop at onStop and restart at onStart.

questions.question: What does the `5_000` in this code mean?
options: Upstream keeps running 5 s after the last subscriber leaves
Upstream collection starts 5 s after the first subscriber appears
The upstream is cancelled if it doesn't emit a value within 5 s
New subscribers get every value emitted in the previous 5 s
questions.explanation: `WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis)` stops the upstream only after there have been no subscribers for that long. A rotation unsubscribes for a moment, and the 5 s window keeps the upstream alive so the new UI gets the current state without re-running the query. The timeout does not delay the start, and StateFlow replays only the current value.

questions.question: When does `println("after")` run?
options: Only once the lifecycle reaches DESTROYED
Right after both collectors are launched
Every time the lifecycle drops below STARTED
Never: repeatOnLifecycle doesn't return
questions.explanation: `repeatOnLifecycle` suspends the calling coroutine: it runs the block each time the lifecycle reaches STARTED and cancels it on STOPPED, over and over. It only returns when the lifecycle is DESTROYED, so code after it effectively runs at teardown. Putting work after it by mistake is a common bug; it does return, though, so "never" is wrong.

questions.question: The UI collects with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`, and the app has been in the background for a minute. With which `stateIn` strategies is the upstream still running? Select all that apply.
options: SharingStarted.Eagerly
SharingStarted.Lazily, after a first subscriber had appeared
SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)
SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed() with the default timeout of 0
questions.explanation: `Eagerly` starts at once and `Lazily` starts at the first subscriber, and both then keep the upstream running until the scope is cancelled, regardless of subscribers. `WhileSubscribed` stops the upstream once no one has collected for the timeout, which after a minute in the background has passed for both 0 and 5 s. That is why `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` is the usual default for UI state.

questions.question: Which are good practices when unit-testing a ViewModel's StateFlow with kotlinx-coroutines-test? Select all that apply.
options: Use `runTest`, which skips `delay` calls by using virtual time
Call `Dispatchers.setMain(...)` with a test dispatcher and reset it afterwards
Inject dispatchers instead of hard-coding `Dispatchers.IO` in the ViewModel
Use `Thread.sleep()` so the StateFlow has time to update
Wrap assertions in `runBlocking` inside `runTest` to flush coroutines
questions.explanation: `viewModelScope` uses `Dispatchers.Main`, which does not exist in a JVM test, so it must be replaced with `setMain`. Injected dispatchers let the test pass a dispatcher sharing the test scheduler, and `runTest` makes delays instant. Sleeping or nesting `runBlocking` does not advance the virtual clock and makes tests slow and flaky; use `advanceUntilIdle()` or `runCurrent()` instead.

questions.question: This test fails: `items` is still empty. `Dispatchers.Main` is set to a test dispatcher. What is the cause?
options: Nothing subscribes, so WhileSubscribed never starts the upstream; value stays initial
advanceUntilIdle can't advance viewModelScope, because viewModelScope always runs on Dispatchers.IO
stateIn always skips the first value from the upstream, so the fake's list is never delivered
runTest finishes before the ViewModel has been created, so the assertion reads a stale object
questions.explanation: With `WhileSubscribed`, the upstream only runs while someone collects; reading `.value` does not count as a subscription. Start a collector in the test, e.g. `backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect() }`, or use a library like Turbine. `viewModelScope` uses Main, which the test replaced, so advancing does work.

questions.question: A test collects `vm.uiState` into a list and expects `[Idle, Loading, Success]`, but gets `[Idle, Success]`. The ViewModel sets Loading and then Success with no suspension point in between. Why?
options: StateFlow is conflated, and the collector didn't run between the two assignments
The test collector drops the first state it receives after subscribing, by design of collect
MutableStateFlow only emits a value when its class differs from the class of the previous one
Loading was set on another dispatcher, and the test dispatcher filters out foreign emissions
questions.explanation: StateFlow keeps only the latest value; a collector that is resumed after both assignments reads Success and never sees Loading. This is correct behaviour for state, so tests should not rely on observing every intermediate value. Assert on the final state, or model must-see emissions differently, rather than expecting StateFlow to replay a history.

questions.question: Calling `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` on a plain cold `Flow<T>` (not a `StateFlow`) requires you to pass an `initialValue`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Compose state must have a value on the first composition, before the flow has emitted. A `StateFlow` already has one (`.value`), so its overload needs no argument, but for a plain `Flow` you must provide `initialValue`. This is one reason ViewModels usually expose `StateFlow` via `stateIn`.

questions.question: What's wrong with exposing state like this?
questions.code:
fun uiState(): StateFlow<UiState> =
    repo.observe()
        .map(::toUiState)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, UiState())
options: Each call starts a new StateFlow and upstream collection living in viewModelScope
stateIn can only be called while the ViewModel's init block runs, so this throws at runtime
Nothing: stateIn caches its result per scope, so repeated calls return the same StateFlow
It throws because viewModelScope is already active when the function gets called from the UI
questions.explanation: `stateIn` is not memoized: every call shares the upstream anew in `viewModelScope`, so each recomposition or caller can start another collection that keeps running. Expose a single `val uiState = ... .stateIn(...)` property instead. There is no rule tying `stateIn` to `init`.
